lesson.title: The Alphabet & Je m'appelle
lesson.subtitle: Spelling your name: w is double-v, y is i-grec

hook.title: Twenty-Six Letters, Some Wearing Disguises
hook.content: The French alphabet is the English alphabet with a French voice — but a few letters have new names: w is double-v (double vé), y is i-grec (Greek i), z is zède, g is gé and j is ji. When a reservation requires spelling, French spells: B comme Béatrice.

footnotes.title: comme-spelling
footnotes.content: French spells names by analogy: 'M comme Marie, A comme Anita…' — the word comme ('like') does the pointing. Keep a small stock of proper nouns ready.

pattern.title: je m'appelle — I Call Myself
pattern.content: Introductions are reflexive: je m'appelle Marie — 'I call myself Marie'. The se of appeler walks left like every pronoun you've met: je me appelle → je m'appelle (elision again). Comment tu t'appelles ? — how do you call yourself? The whole intro formula is machinery you already own.

footnotes.title: The double-l story
footnotes.content: me + appelle elides to m'appelle. The l is not doubled for fun: je me appelle → je m'appelle — the vowel sacrificed, as always.

pattern.trap_note: Don't say je suis Marie for 'my name is Marie' — that's 'I am Marie' (costume-party French). The French introduce by the calling verb: je m'appelle.

exercises.prompt: Match each letter with its French name:
exercises.target_answer: double vé, i grec, gé, zède
exercises.explanation: double-v is honest: the letter IS two vees. English renamed it double-u and didn't update the shape.
The reflexive formula: je m'appelle. je suis Marie would be a costume declaration.

exercises.prompt: Elide it: 'je me appelle' → the written form:
exercises.explanation: me loses its vowel before a — the apostrophe law, third sighting.

exercises.idea: you're asking a new acquaintance their name (informal)
cues: tu + the reflexive pronoun te → t'

vocab_hints.note: from Latin quam modum? — 'by what measure'

exercises.explanation: te walks left and elides, exactly like me did. The machinery is identical — only the person changes.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.meaning: My name is Alex, and you? (formal)
cues: et vous ? — the polite return question
exercises.explanation: et vous ? — the formal return. With a friend: et toi ?
exercises.affirmation: You kept the apostrophe in m'appelle — the vowel's tombstone stands.

summary.outcome: Spell with French letter names, introduce yourself with je m'appelle, and ask it back with the elided reflexive.

use_example.english: My name is Alex. And you?

summary.takeaway: Introductions are reflexive and elided — the same pronoun machinery, pointed at yourself.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([5021] Think the N): see how The Alphabet & Je m'appelle leads directly into Think the N.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "What's your name" in French:
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Comment tu t'appelles" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of The Alphabet & Je m'appelle.

appeler.context_translation: My name is Marie (I call myself Marie).
appeler.etymology_derivation: ad + pellere 'to drive toward' — an appeal drives someone toward you. je m'appelle: I call myself.

cest.english_meaning: it is; this is; that is
cest.etymology_derivation: ce ('that') + est — the elision French performs constantly: a vowel before a vowel loses its tail.

vous.etymology_derivation: Latin vōs 'you all' promoted to politeness — the same T–V ladder as German Sie and English's lost 'ye'.
